issues.issue: The Agreement is recited as "made by and between" EGL and the Borrower, yet only EGL grants the guarantee, so whether Essar Steel Minnesota is a bound party is unclear against Section 2.02(d) and (f), which impose affirmative obligations on the Borrower. The preamble also names the Facility Agent as the party in whose favor it is made while the recitals speak of the ratable benefit of the Lenders.

The recital states the guarantee is delivered "for the ratable benefit of the Lenders," which sits against the operative preamble and Section 4.15, under which the Agreement runs in favor of the Facility Agent and confers rights only on Lenders. A party could argue the recital controls who may enforce.

Wholesale incorporation of the Credit Agreement's defined terms cannot be squared with Section 4.14 (Entire Agreement), which declares this Agreement alone the entire agreement and supersedes all prior agreements on the subject matter. Which document supplies meaning is then contestable.

"Agreement" is defined as subject to being "restated, amended, supplemented or otherwise modified from time to time," but the instrument contains no amendment provision and Section 4.01 points only to Section 4.12 (Notices) for written instruments. How an amendment is validly made is left open.

The catch-all "all other obligations and liabilities of the Borrower ... which may arise under, out of, or in connection with" the Loan Documents follows an enumeration of principal, interest and LC Exposure, leaving the guaranteed universe without a boundary. Section 1.02(e) expressly disclaims ejusdem generis, sharpening the fight over scope.

A "Deficiency" is what is "determined by the Borrower or the Required Lenders," giving two independent determiners with no rule for conflicting or competing determinations and no standard of determination. Whether either determination binds the Guarantor is unresolved.

Clause (ii) does not read grammatically onto the lead-in ("shortfall ... required: ... any increase in the cost of the Project") and largely duplicates clause (i), which already covers costs above US$1,097,000,000 outside a Permitted Project Change. The two limbs cannot be given distinct content as drafted.

The release condition turns on offtake agreements "in form and substance and for a term ... reasonably acceptable" to 66 2/3% Lenders and on an offtaker "reasonably acceptable" to them, with no objective benchmark or outside date. Whether the guarantee is ever released is thus committed to a reasonableness standard a court would have to construe.

The proviso obliges Lenders only to "negotiate in good faith" over a "draft pellet purchase agreement that would be reasonably acceptable," an agreement to agree with no standard of compliance or consequence for failure. It is also a Lender obligation buried inside a definition.

"Material adverse effect on the business, financial condition, operations or performance or properties of the Guarantor since the date of this Agreement" supplies no benchmark or magnitude for materiality and the trailing "since the date of this Agreement" has no clear grammatical anchor. The term drives paragraphs (a), (c), (d) and (m) of Article III.

"Obligations" is defined as the Borrower Obligations, while "Borrower Obligations" is itself defined by reference to "the Obligations (as defined in the Credit Agreement)," creating a circular definitional loop between this provision and the Borrower Obligations definition. Which "Obligations" is meant in Sections 4.02(c) and elsewhere is then uncertain.

The clause is truncated — "words importing any gender include the other" omits the noun it governs — so the rule has no stated object. A mechanical omission of this kind leaves the interpretive rule incomplete on its face.

This rule abolishes ejusdem generis and expressio unius for every list in the instrument, which cannot be comfortably squared with enumerations elsewhere that appear closed — the two-limb "Deficiency" definition and the two permitted funding forms in Section 2.02(d). Whether those lists are exhaustive is thrown into doubt.

"Permitted successors and assigns ... not prohibited by the terms hereof" depends on the assignment rules, but Sections 4.03 and 4.15 state different consent requirements for the same act. What counts as a permitted assign is therefore indeterminate.

Section 1.03 makes this Agreement govern over any conflicting Loan Document, yet Section 1.01, Section 2.02(d), the last sentence of Section 2.03 (Credit Agreement Section 6.07) and Section 4.12 all subordinate this Agreement's operation to the Credit Agreement. Which instrument controls in a conflict is left genuinely open.

The three guarantee periods do not fit together: clause (i) runs only until the Credit Agreement conditions in "Sections 4.01 through 4.02" are satisfied (skipping Section 4.03), clause (iii) begins only at the Commercial Operations Date, leaving an interval covered by nothing but the Deficiency undertaking, and the $250,000,000 cap is expressed to apply only "under this clause (iii)." Whether EGL's exposure is capped at all, and when, is the central construction question.

The temporal limits on clauses (i) and (ii) cannot be squared with Section 2.01(d), which says the guarantee "contained in this Section 2.01" remains in full force until the earlier of the EGL Guarantee Release Date or payment in full. One provision ends the guarantee on satisfaction of conditions precedent; the other keeps it alive.

The sentence is broken — "the obligations of the Guarantor hereunder are primary and notwithstanding the obligations of any other Person providing any Guarantee, Collateral or other assurance" leaves the "notwithstanding" limb without a predicate. What effect the other credit support has on EGL's primary liability cannot be read off the words.

The savings cap is measured by "applicable federal and state laws relating to fraudulent conveyances," although the Guarantor is a Cayman Islands company and the instrument is New York-governed, so which body of law fixes the ceiling is unstated. It also purports to cap liability "under the other Loan Documents," reaching beyond this Agreement.

Termination at "the earlier of" the EGL Guarantee Release Date or payment in full cannot be squared with Section 2.01(a), which fixes distinct start and end points for each of the three guarantee limbs, nor with Section 2.06's reinstatement. Read literally the guarantee can expire while Borrower Obligations remain outstanding.

The sentence is mechanically defective: "The Borrower shall notify the Guarantor ... to the extent a Deficiency at any time exists and that the Guarantor provides to the Borrower the amount of the Deficiency" omits the operative demand verb. Whether the notice imposes a funding demand, and on what terms, is unclear from the words.

The trigger "[i]f no action is taken by the Borrower to notify the Guarantor" sets no period within which the Borrower must act before the Facility Agent may step in. It is also unstated whether the Engineering Consultant certification is a condition to the notice's validity.

The statement that the Facility Agent and Lenders have "no obligation to issue a notice of Deficiency" sits against Section 2.02(a), under which the Borrower "shall notify" the Guarantor, and against Section 2.01(a)(ii), which makes the Guarantor's funding obligation arise only when it "receives notice of such Deficiency." Read together, the Deficiency obligation may never be triggered.

Exculpation "for demanding insufficient funds" cannot easily be squared with Section 2.01(a)(ii), which obliges the Guarantor to provide "the full and complete amount of any Deficiency." Whether the Guarantor owes the notified amount or the actual shortfall is left open.

The provision says funds "shall be provided by way of" a capital contribution "or" an Unsecured Subordinated Promoter Loan without saying who elects between the two, while Sections 2.02(d) and (f) speak only of what happens "[i]f the Guarantor decides." Section 2.02 also skips subsections (c) and (e), leaving the procedure visibly incomplete.

The Borrower is required to "increase its charter capital," a concept with no application to a Minnesota limited liability company, whose interests Section 2.02(f) calls "Equity Interests." What corporate act the Borrower must take is therefore uncertain.

"[T]o pay the cost or cost that has created the Deficiency" is garbled and does not identify whose obligation the payment is or which costs qualify. The defect matters because the Deficiency definition speaks of Project costs in the aggregate rather than particular costs.

The same garbled phrase "the cost or cost that has created the Deficiency" governs application of promoter loan proceeds, leaving the permitted use undefined. It also does not address application where the loan exceeds or falls short of the notified Deficiency.

Subrogation is barred until all Guarantor Obligations are paid in full, no Letter of Credit is outstanding and Total Commitments are terminated, which cannot be squared with Section 2.01(d), under which the guarantee ends on the earlier EGL Guarantee Release Date. Whether the bar survives release of the guarantee is unresolved.

This sentence lets the Guarantor be reimbursed if the payment is permitted under Section 6.07 of the Credit Agreement, contradicting the flat prohibition on contribution and reimbursement in the first sentence of Section 2.03. Section 1.03, which makes this Agreement control over the Credit Agreement, makes the priority between them harder still.

The section, headed "with respect to the Borrower Obligations," repeatedly authorizes the Facility Agent and Lenders to amend, waive, surrender or release "the Guarantor Obligations" while declaring that the Guarantor "shall remain obligated hereunder." Whether a release of the Guarantor Obligations discharges EGL or leaves it liable cannot be read off the text.

The interposed exception — "except to the extent set forth in, and for the benefit of the parties to, the agreements and instruments governing such Lien or guarantee" — leaves "such Lien" without an antecedent and obscures the sentence's operation. What duty, if any, the Facility Agent owes as to collateral is thus uncertain.

The waiver extends to notice of any event "affecting any term of a Guaranteed Obligation," but "Guaranteed Obligation" is nowhere defined; the defined terms are "Borrower Obligations" and "Guarantor Obligations." The reach of the notice waiver turns on which is meant.

The Guarantor waives "demand for payment" and notice of default, yet Section 2.01(a)(ii) conditions the Deficiency obligation on receipt of a Deficiency notice and Section 2.05 later contemplates the Facility Agent "making any demand hereunder." Whether any demand is a precondition to liability is left in doubt.

The carve-out preserving "a defense of payment or performance" sits against limb (iii), which sweeps away "any other circumstance whatsoever" that might discharge the Guarantor. Which defenses survive the absolute-guarantee language is a genuine construction question.

Defining "demand" to "include" the commencement of legal proceedings does not say what else constitutes a demand or whether a demand must satisfy the written-notice requirements of Section 4.12. The inclusive definition leaves the trigger for the Guarantor's payment obligation unfixed.

Reinstatement is triggered only by the insolvency, bankruptcy or reorganization "of the Guarantor," although the payments that would be clawed back are the Borrower's and the Borrower Obligations definition expressly contemplates a Borrower bankruptcy. The apparent substitution of Guarantor for Borrower guts the clause.

The undertaking to pay "without set-off or counterclaim" cannot be squared with Section 2.05, which preserves "a defense of payment or performance" to the Guarantor. Whether the Guarantor may withhold on that ground is left open.

The lead-in casts everything in Article III as representations and warranties repeated on every representation date, yet paragraphs (l) through (o) are forward-looking covenants — one of which binds the Borrower, not the Guarantor. The two characterizations cannot both be given effect.

The absolute statement that "no consent or authorization of, filing with, notice to or other act" is required cannot be squared with Article III(c)'s reference to stamp duty and registration charges "already paid" or with Section 4.13's Patriot Act and know-your-customer requirements. The scope of the representation is contestable.

The representation that performance "will not result in the creation or imposition of any Lien on any asset of the Guarantor" sits against Section 2.03, which creates a trust over subrogation proceeds, and Section 4.04, which grants set-off rights over the Guarantor's deposits. Whether those arrangements are Liens is a question the two provisions raise together.

The representation that no stamp duty, registration charges or statutory levies remain payable "except for those already paid" cannot be squared with Section 4.02(b), by which the Guarantor agrees to pay stamp, excise and sales taxes "which may be payable or determined to be payable with respect to this Agreement." One assumes none are owed; the other assumes they may be.

The litigation representation is confined to proceedings "with respect to this Agreement or any of the transactions contemplated hereby," leaving all other litigation against the Guarantor outside it even though Material Adverse Effect is defined company-wide. The clause also contains the error "reasonably be expect to result."

"[U]nreasonably small capital with which to conduct the business" as it "is proposed to be conducted" has no measurable boundary and depends on unstated projections. The solvency representation turns on a phrase the clause never defines.

"[S]hall at all time rank at least pari passu" is a continuing covenant cast among representations, and "senior Indebtedness of the Guarantor" is not defined in this Agreement. Whether it warrants a present fact or promises future ranking is unclear.
"[S]ubstantial Equity Interest" fixes no percentage or other threshold, so the representation has no ascertainable boundary. Nothing elsewhere in the Agreement supplies a measure.

The sentence is mechanically defective — "none of the or governors or managers of the Guarantor" omits a noun — so the class of persons covered is not stated. The scope of the Reserve Bank of India relationship representation turns on that missing word.

The opening cross-reference, "[i]n addition to the requirements of Section 4.13," points to the Patriot Act provision, which imposes no willful-defaulter requirement under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 of India. The cross-reference cannot be given effect as written.

"[E]xpeditious and effective steps for the removal" of a willful defaulter sets no time limit and no measure of effectiveness, and does not say who identifies the person. Whether the Guarantor has complied is not testable against the words.

The Guarantor covenants that it "has not used and shall not use any part of the Facility," although the Facility is extended to the Borrower and the Guarantor never draws on it, and "agents acting or benefitting in any capacity" has no boundary. The clause's application to a guarantor is doubtful on its face.

The waiver is framed around immunity "attributed to the Borrower" although it is the Guarantor's immunity that is being waived, an apparent substitution of the wrong defined party. Whose immunity is surrendered turns on that word.

"No Default in respect of the Guarantor" uses a term defined in the Credit Agreement by reference to Events of Default of the Borrower, so what a Guarantor Default is cannot be determined from either instrument. Section 4.01's reference to acquiescence in "any Default or Event of Default" carries the same uncertainty.

The representation is qualified to information "taken as a whole" and "true in all material respects," and "Confidential Information Material" is not defined in this Agreement. What statements are actually warranted is difficult to fix.

"[S]ubstantially more favorable" terms in favor of a non-Lender Project Lender is a comparison with no stated metric, and "guarantee or other support" is open-ended. Compliance cannot be measured from the provision's own words.

Notice is owed of any development that "would reasonably be expected to have or result in" a Material Adverse Effect, a standard resting on the already unbounded Material Adverse Effect definition and on a Responsible Officer's knowledge. When the five-Business-Day clock starts is contestable.

The proviso that the restriction "shall not apply to an arms length sale or disposal of its assets or properties" swallows the prohibition it qualifies, since virtually any disposal could be styled arm's length. Read literally the covenant restricts nothing.

The paragraph speaks of "either Guarantor" and "either Guarantee Agreement," which cannot be squared with the preamble and Section 1.01, where "Guarantor" means EGL alone and "Agreement" means this Guarantee Agreement only. It also imposes the obligation on the Borrower in an instrument otherwise granting EGL's guarantee.

"[T]he Parent" is used but nowhere defined in this Agreement, which defines only EGL as Guarantor; the term comes from the Credit Agreement recitals. Whom the Borrower may pay dividends to is therefore not fixed by these words.

Waiver is excepted only "by a written instrument pursuant to Section 4.12," but Section 4.12 is the Notices provision and contains no waiver or amendment mechanism. How a binding written waiver is given cannot be determined from the cross-reference.

Enforcement costs are recoverable only by the Facility Agent and only its counsel's fees are named, although the "Borrower Obligations" definition contemplates fees of counsel to the Facility Agent "or the Lenders." On an expressio unius reading the Lenders' own enforcement costs are excluded.

The undertaking to pay "any and all stamp, excise, sales or other taxes" payable with respect to this Agreement cannot be squared with Article III(c), which represents that no stamp duty, registration charges or statutory levies remain due except those already paid. One provision presupposes the liability the other denies.

Survival is expressed as running past "repayment of the Obligations," a term Section 1.01 defines to mean different things for the Borrower and the Guarantor, so the survival trigger is not fixed. It also purports to survive amounts payable under the Credit Agreement rather than this Agreement.

This proviso bars assignment by the Guarantor without "the prior written consent of the Facility Agent," while Section 4.15 bars the same act without the consent of "the Facility Agent and the Lenders." The two consent requirements cannot both govern.

Set-off is exercisable "while an Event of Default shall have occurred and be continuing," a term defined in the Credit Agreement by reference to the Borrower, and this Agreement defines no Guarantor default. Whether a Guarantor's own failure to pay triggers the right is unclear.

Section 4.08 states that this Agreement "and the other Loan Documents" represent the parties' agreement, while Section 4.14 states that this Agreement alone constitutes the entire agreement and supersedes all prior agreements on the subject matter. The two integration clauses cannot both be given effect.

The submission says proceedings "may be instituted in or (other than by the Guarantor) removed to" the New York courts without saying whether that forum is exclusive, and the last sentence of Section 4.10(b) preserves proceedings against the Guarantor "in any other venue where assets ... may be found." Whether the Guarantor may be sued elsewhere is left open.

The provision says the Guarantor "shall irrevocably designate" Essar Americas, Inc. as process agent but records no acceptance by that agent and no time by which the designation must be made. Whether service on it is effective from the date of the Agreement is uncertain.

The replacement process agent must have "offices in [New York]" — an unresolved bracketed placeholder left in the executed text. Whether the bracketed words are operative terms is a construction question on the face of the clause.

Preserving the Lenders' right to sue "in any other venue where assets of the Guarantor may be found" cuts against Section 4.10(a)'s submission to the Manhattan courts and its venue and forum non conveniens waivers. Which provision fixes the forum is contestable.

Notices are "effective when received," but Section 4.12's delivery rule permits telefax only "with a confirmation copy by internationally recognized courier service," so it is unstated whether receipt of the fax or of the courier copy fixes effectiveness. The timing matters to the Deficiency notices under Section 2.02.

Notices go to "the address of the Guarantor set forth below its signature," yet one executed signature page leaves the Address for Notices block blank and the other gives a Mauritius address for a Cayman Islands company. Where valid notice to EGL may be given is not settled by the instrument.

The sentence is internally garbled — "Each Lender and the Facility Agent, when appointed hereunder, (for itself and not on behalf of any Lender)" — and the Facility Agent is not appointed under this Agreement at all. Who gives the Patriot Act notice, and in what capacity, cannot be read off the words.

Declaring this Agreement the "entire agreement" superseding all prior agreements cannot be squared with Section 4.08, which treats this Agreement and the other Loan Documents together as the parties' agreement, or with Section 1.01's incorporation of Credit Agreement definitions. Whether the Credit Agreement remains part of the bargain is thrown into doubt.

This binding-effect sentence duplicates Section 4.03 but describes a different set of beneficiaries — "the parties hereto and their successors and assigns" rather than the Facility Agent and the Lenders. Which formulation governs succession is unresolved.

This proviso conditions assignment on the consent of "the Facility Agent and the Lenders," while Section 4.03 conditions the identical act on the consent of the Facility Agent alone. The two restrictions cannot both control.

The clause is missing its verb — "the Guarantor shall not the right to assign or transfer its rights and obligations hereunder" — so the prohibition is not grammatically stated. A court would have to supply the omitted word to give the proviso effect.

The clause reserves benefit to "the Lenders," who are not signatories to this Agreement (the Facility Agent signs on their behalf), and excludes the Issuing Bank and other Secured Parties, although the Credit Agreement defines the Guarantee Agreements as given in favor of "the Lenders and the other Secured Parties." Who may enforce the guarantee is therefore contestable.
